extracted.intended_audience: sovereigns, rulers, political philosophers, and students of natural and Christian political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for sovereign government and public worship: how a sovereign should apply punishments and rewards, choose counsellors and commanders, and regulate public and divine worship (natural and Christian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of punishing is not revenge, and discharge of choler; but correction, either of the offender, or of others by his example; the severest punishments are to be inflicted for those crimes, that are of most danger to the publique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe punishments for crimes most dangerous to the commonwealth: those proceeding from malice to the established government; contempt of justice; acts provoking public indignation; and acts which, if unpunished, seem authorised (e.g., crimes by sons, servants, or favourites of men in authority). Punishment aims at correction and deterrence, not mere revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lenity for crimes of infirmity
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes of infirmity (proceeding from great provocation, great fear, great need, or ignorance whether the fact be a great crime) allow many times for lenity, without prejudice to the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is reasonable provocation, fear, necessity, or ignorance, sovereigns should consider mercy; lenity is required by the law of nature when it does not harm the commonwealth. Prefer punishing leaders/teachers rather than the poor seduced people, since punishing the ignorant may blame the sovereign for lack of instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards applied for public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewards belong to the sovereign to be applied so that they produce benefit to the commonwealth; their use and end is to recompense past service and encourage others to serve and improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward those who have well served the commonwealth as economically as possible while still encouraging faithful service and skill development. Do not use money or preferment to buy off ambitious popular subjects (that is not a reward but a bribe driven by fear), since it fosters more ambition and mischief and may increase the danger of civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding public disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against the duty of the sovereign to reward those who aspire to greatness by disturbing the peace of their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than buying peace from ambitious troublemakers, oppose the beginnings of such men even at a little danger; rewarding them encourages imitators (comparing ambition to the Hydra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of counsellors
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign should choose counsellors who are in every kind the most able; those who have the least hope of benefit by giving evil counsel, and most knowledge of matters conducive to the peace and defence of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good counsellors are not chosen by lot or inheritance. Signs of untrustworthy advisers include soothing the people over unreasonable grievances and those whose estates cannot meet accustomed expenses. Preference for those with extensive practice in political matters and a track record of good effects. Private, premeditated advice given separately by each counsellor is preferable to orations in assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit local information for domestic matters
rubrics_metrics.description: For internal laws and the ease and benefit of subjects, take counsel from general informations and complaints of the people of each province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locals know their own wants best; sovereign should diligently notice these demands so long as they do not derogate from essential rights of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities and popularity of commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: A commander in chief must be industrious, valiant, affable, liberal and fortunate to gain an opinion both of sufficiency and of loving his soldiers (popularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity among soldiers breeds desire and courage to serve and protects necessary severity in discipline. However, the sovereign must be cautious: a popular commander can be dangerous to sovereign power if the commander and his cause are loved against the sovereign. If the sovereign is himself popular, then a subject's popularity poses less danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign right to procure public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sovereign hath the same right, in procuring the safety of his people, that any particular man can have in procuring the safety of his own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of nations and the law of nature coincide in giving sovereigns authority analogous to individual self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subjects in the kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects in the kingdom of God are those who believe there is a God that governeth the world, have hope of rewards and fear of punishments; atheists and those who deny God's providence are to be understood as enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in God's governance and receptivity to divine precepts (reason, revelation, prophecy) constitutes membership in God's kingdom; mere denial or unbelief excludes one from being a subject in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of promulgation for law
rubrics_metrics.description: To the nature of laws belongeth a sufficient and clear promulgation, such as may take away the excuse of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God's laws (like human laws) must be made manifest to be laws; when God speaks, the mode of promulgation (reason, revelation, prophetic voice) affects who is bound and how universal the law is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold Word of God and corresponding hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: God declareth his laws three ways: by the dictates of natural reason (rational), by revelation (sense supernatural), and by the voice of some man to whom, by miracles, he procures credit (prophetique). To these correspond a triple hearing: right reason, sense supernatural, and faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revelation and prophetic speech are not universally binding in the same way as natural reason; universal law requires manifest promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a twofold kingdom of God: Natural, where he governs those acknowledging his providence by natural reason; and Prophetique, where he governed a chosen nation by positive laws given through prophets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between duties derivable from natural reason and those arising from positive, prophetic law when determining obligations of subjects and commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of God's sovereignty derived from omnipotence
rubrics_metrics.description: The right whereby God reigneth over men and punisheth those that break his laws is to be derived, not from his creating them, but from his irresistible power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereignty grounded in power justifies the right to govern and afflict; divine authority is likened to irresistible power rather than merely creation-based gratitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine laws include natural duties and duties of worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine laws or dictats of natural reason concern either the natural duties of one man to another (equity, justice, mercy, humility) or the honour naturally due to our divine sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morall virtues previously discussed form the civil duties; separately, natural reason dictates how to honour and worship God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of honour and worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour consisteth in the inward thought and opinion of the power and goodness of another; worship are the external signs appearing in words and actions through which honour is expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultus (culture/courting) is the labour to gain benefit; worship is courting God by praises, acknowledgements, and acts pleasing to the one worshipped. The internal opinion (honour) grounds external acts (worship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Severall signs and parts of honour
rubrics_metrics.description: From internal honour arise three passions: love (referring to goodness), and hope and fear (relating to power); and three parts of external worship: praise (goodness), magnifying and blessing (power and felicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise and magnifying are expressed by words and actions; the opinion of another's happiness can only be expressed by words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural versus arbitrary worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Some signs of honour (attributes and actions) are naturally so (e.g., good, just, liberall; prayers, thanks, obedience); others are by institution or custom and vary by time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturally honourable signs cannot be properly made dishonourable by human law; arbitrary signs may be commanded or left free by sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanded vs voluntary, public vs private worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary worship may be commanded (required by the one worshipped) or voluntary; worship may be publique (that of the commonwealth) or private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When worship is commanded the obedience is the worship; when voluntary, the worship's value is judged by spectators. Public worship of a commonwealth ought to be uniform to count as a single public worship; private worship, while free in secret, is restrained in public by law and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes to ascribe to God (and what not to ascribe)
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought to attribute to God Existence, and avoid ascribing to him finiteness, parts, place, motion, passions or other properties proper to finite beings; use negative, superlative, or indefinite attributes (Infinite, Eternall, Most High, Good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid theological attributions that circumscribe God within human categories (figure, place, passions). When ascribing will, sight, knowledge to God, do so in ways that do not import human, natural causal mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions that are signs of divine honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayers, thanksgiving, gifts (sacrifices and oblations of the best), refraining from swearing by any but God, speaking considerately of God, well-composed prayers and thanksgivings, public worship, and obedience to his laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These actions should be significant and the best of their kind (e.g., well-composed language, proper offerings), performed publicly as well as privately when reasonable, and aimed at true submission and remembrance of benefits. Disputing God's nature from natural reason is warned against as dishonourable and vain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public worship should be uniform
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonwealth, as one person, ought to exhibit to God but one public worship; public worship's property is to be uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing many sorts of worship emerging from differing private religions means there is no single public worship and the commonwealth lacks a unified religion. Sovereigns may by civil law determine the signs, attributes, and forms of public worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil laws determine public attributes of worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Since words and attributes have signification by agreement and constitution of men, those attributes the sovereign ordaineth in the worship of God are to be taken and used for such by private men in their public worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commonwealth can, by civil law, institute arbitrary signs of honour and require their public observance; private men must follow those ordinances in public worship except where actions are naturally signs of honour or contumely and thus cannot properly be legislated otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on instituting acts as worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all actions are signs by constitution; some are naturally signs of honour or contumely and cannot be made by human power a part of divine worship, while indifferent actions may be ordained by the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human law cannot convert naturally dishonourable acts into worship nor separate naturally honourable behaviour from worship. The scriptural maxim 'It is better to obey God than men' properly applies in the kingdom of God by pact, not by nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural punishments as consequential laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human action begins a chain of consequences; natural punishments are those pains naturally consequent to breaches of the laws of nature (e.g., intemperance punished with disease; rashness with mishaps; injustice with enemies; pride with ruin; cowardice with oppression; negligent princes with rebellion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereigns and subjects should understand that many punishments are natural effects of actions rather than arbitrary afflictions; governance must account for these natural consequences when forming laws and expectations.
